claim: HIV-1 has originated from multiple zoonotic transmissions from apes in the early part of the 20th century.
source: HIV-1 has originated from multiple zoonotic transmissions from apes in the early part of the 20th century (Sharp and Hahn, 2011), one of which gave rise to the worldwide pandemic.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sharp and Hahn, 2011.

claim: HIV-1 group M has diversified into different subtypes at a rate of about 1 in 1000 substitutions per year.
source: This lineage is called group M and has diversified into different subtypes at a rate of about 1 in 1000 substitutions per year (Lemey et al., 2005; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lemey et al., 2005 and Li et al., 2015.

claim: Tens of thousands of HIV-1 group M variants are available in the Los Alamos National Laboratories HIV database.
source: Tens of thousand of HIV-1 group M variants are available in the Los Alamos National Laboratories HIV database (LANL) (Foley et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foley et al., 2013.

claim: During the first few months of an HIV-1 infection, the viral population typically acquires several mutations that mediate escape from cytotoxic T-cells (CTL).
source: During the first few months of an HIV-1 infection, the viral population typically acquires several mutations that mediate escape from cytotoxic T-cells (CTL). The properties and dynamics of these mutations and their effect on epitope presentation and virus control have been extensively studied (Bernardin et al., 2005; Goonetilleke et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2004; Kearney et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on CTL escape mutations.

claim: CTL escape variants often compromise virus replication and have been shown to revert upon transmission of the virus to an HLA mismatched host.
source: Such escape variants often compromise virus replication and have been shown to revert upon transmission of the virus to a human leukocyte antigen (HLA) mismatched host (Brockman et al., 2010; Leslie et al., 2004; Li et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brockman et al., 2010; Leslie et al., 2004; Li et al., 2007.

claim: The study performed whole-genome deep sequencing of HIV-1 populations in 9 untreated patients, with 6-12 longitudinal samples per patient spanning 5-8 years of infection.
source: We performed whole-genome deep sequencing of HIV-1 populations in 9 untreated patients, with 6-12 longitudinal samples per patient spanning 5-8 years of infection.
evidence: The claim describes the study design and is directly stated in the abstract.

claim: Patterns of minor diversity are reproducible between patients and mirror global HIV-1 diversity.
source: We show that patterns of minor diversity are reproducible between patients and mirror global HIV-1 diversity, suggesting a universal landscape of fitness costs that control diversity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the study, particularly in Figure 4.

claim: Reversions towards the ancestral HIV-1 sequence are observed throughout infection and account for almost one third of all sequence changes.
source: Reversions towards the ancestral HIV-1 sequence are observed throughout infection and account for almost one third of all sequence changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the study, particularly in Figure 6.

claim: Reversion rates depend strongly on conservation.
source: Reversion rates depend strongly on conservation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Frequent recombination limits linkage disequilibrium to about 100bp in most of the genome.
source: Frequent recombination limits linkage disequilibrium to about 100bp in most of the genome, but strong hitch-hiking due to short range linkage limits diversity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The study included nine HIV-1-infected patients who were diagnosed in Sweden between 1990 and 2003.
source: The study included nine HIV-1-infected patients who were diagnosed in Sweden between 1990 and 2003.
evidence: The claim describes the study cohort and is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Data from two additional patients (p4 and p7) were excluded from analysis because of suspected superinfection and failure to amplify early samples with low virus levels, respectively.
source: Data from two additional patients (p4 and p7) were excluded from analysis because of suspected superinfection and failure to amplify early samples with low virus levels, respectively.
evidence: The claim describes exclusion criteria applied in the study.

claim: The patients were selected to have a relatively well-defined time of infection and to have been treatment-naive for a minimum of 5 years.
source: The patients were selected to have a relatively well-defined time of infection and to have been treatment-naive for a minimum of 5 years.
evidence: The claim describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: All patients progressed to moderate-to-severe immunosuppression during the study period.
source: All patients progressed to moderate-to-severe immunosuppression during the study period.
evidence: The claim is supported by CD4 count data provided in the text.

claim: Of the nine patients, eight were males, seven were men who have sex with men (MSM), two were heterosexually infected (HET), and eight were infected in Sweden.
source: Of the nine patients, eight were males, seven were men who have sex with men (MSM), two were heterosexually infected (HET), and eight were infected in Sweden.
evidence: The claim describes demographic characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: The median plasma HIV-1 RNA level was 12,000 copies/ml for the samples with available data on RNA levels.
source: The median plasma HIV-1 RNA level was 12,000 copies/ml for the samples with available data on RNA levels.
evidence: The claim reports a measured value from the study samples.

claim: Viral RNA was extracted from 400 μl patient plasma and used for one-step RT-PCR amplification with six overlapping primer sets that span almost the complete HIV-1 genome.
source: Briefly, viral RNA was extracted from 400 μl patient plasma and used for one-step RT-PCR amplification with six overlapping primer sets that span almost the complete HIV-1 genome, similar to the strategy developed by Gall et al. (2012).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq platform.
source: Sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq platform and sequence reads were quality filtered and assembled using an in-house data processing pipeline.
evidence: The claim describes the sequencing technology used.

claim: Approximately 100 million reads passed the quality filtering.
source: In total, approximately 100 million reads passed the quality filtering.
evidence: The claim reports the total number of quality-filtered reads.

claim: The median template cDNA recovery efficiency was 30%.
source: Comparison with routine plasma HIV-1 RNA level measurements performed at time of sampling showed that the median template complementary DNA (cDNA) recovery efficiency was 30%.
evidence: The claim reports a measured efficiency from control experiments.

claim: After quality filtering, PCR and sequencing errors never exceeded 0.3% of reads covering a particular position.
source: After quality filtering, PCR and sequencing errors never exceeded 0.3% of reads covering a particular position.
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments using plasmid clones, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of HIV-1 genomes that contributed to each sequencing library was quantified by PCR-limiting dilution with a median of 120 (quartiles: 50–500).
source: We quantified the number of HIV-1 genomes that contributed to each sequencing library by PCR-limiting dilution (median: 120 quartiles: 50–500).
evidence: The claim reports results from limiting dilution experiments.

claim: Less than 10% of reads had experienced RT-PCR recombination in control experiments using mixtures of two cultured virus populations.
source: Control experiments using mixtures of two cultured virus populations showed that less than 10% of reads had experienced RT-PCR recombination.
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments described in the text.

claim: A web application was developed to explore the data set interactively and visualize the patterns of HIV-1 evolution in the study patients.
source: To facilitate reuse of our data, we developed a web application to explore the data set interactively and visualize the patterns of HIV-1 evolution in the study patients.
evidence: The claim describes a resource created as part of the study.

claim: The web application is available at hiv.tuebingen.mpg.de.
source: We hope that this web application, available at hiv.tuebingen.mpg.de, will encourage others to further analyze these data.
evidence: The claim provides the URL for accessing the web application.

claim: In most patients, the virus populations were initially homogeneous and diversified over the years.
source: In most patients, the virus populations were initially homogeneous and diversified over the years, as expected for an infection with a single or small number of similar founder viruses (Keele et al., 2008; Salazar-Gonzalez et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and citations to previous work.

claim: In two patients, p3 and p10, the first sample displayed diversity consistent with the transmission of several variants from the same donor.
source: In two patients, p3 and p10, the first sample displayed diversity consistent with the transmission of several variants from the same donor, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rate of divergence varies by about a factor of 10 along the genome.
source: The rate of divergence varies by about a factor of 10 along the genome, but is consistent with typically about 1.5-fold differences across patients (standard deviation of log2(fold change) 0.6 ± 0.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The overall pattern of the rate of mutation accumulation agrees with a recent map of HIV genome-wide variation from a population perspective and correlates well with entropy in a large HIV-1 group M alignment (Spearman's p = 0.7 after the same smoothing).
source: The overall pattern of the rate of mutation accumulation agrees with a recent map of HIV genome-wide variation from a population perspective (Li et al., 2015) and correlates well with entropy in a large HIV-1 group M alignment (Spearman's p = 0.7 after the same smoothing).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published data and correlation analysis.

claim: Correlation between intrapatient diversity and cross-sectional diversity increases reproducibly throughout the infection, reaching about 0.4–0.5 after about 8 years.
source: As diversity increases within patients, it tends to accumulate at positions that are not conserved, resulting in a rank correlation of about 0.4–0.5 after about 8 years.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For the least conserved positions, the fraction of sites showing intrapatient variation at a level of at least 1% increased steadily to about 20% after 8 years.
source: For the least conserved positions, this fraction increased steadily to about 20% after 8 years, while less than 1% of the most conserved sites shows variation above the 1% level.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Less than 1% of the most conserved sites shows variation above the 1% level.
source: For the least conserved positions, this fraction increased steadily to about 20% after 8 years, while less than 1% of the most conserved sites shows variation above the 1% level.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Synonymous divergence varied very little between different genomic regions indicating random accumulation of synonymous mutations.
source: Divergence at synonymous sites, however, varied very little between different genomic regions indicating random accumulation of synonymous mutations (rather than positive selection).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Diversity at nonsynonymous sites saturates after about 2–4 years.
source: Diversity at nonsynonymous sites (solid lines) saturates after about 2–4 years, suggesting that nonsynonymous SNPs either stay at low frequency because they are deleterious or rapidly increase in frequency and fix without contributing much to diversity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a strong anti-correlation between synonymous diversity and nonsynonymous divergence.
source: Indeed, we observe a strong anti-correlation between synonymous diversity and nonsynonymous divergence, which is further quantified in Figure 5C.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Synonymous mutations are strongly underrepresented at higher frequencies compared to nonsynonymous mutations.
source: While the spectra agree for frequencies below 20%, synonymous mutations are strongly underrepresented at higher frequencies (Fisher's exact test at frequency 0.5, p-value <10-10).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The about five-fold excess of nonsynonymous over synonymous SNPs at high frequencies shows that the majority of common nonsynonymous mutations spread due to positive selection.
source: The about five-fold excess of nonsynonymous over synonymous SNPs at high frequencies (see Figure 5D) shows that the majority of common nonsynonymous mutations spread due to positive selection.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A significant enrichment by a factor 1.9 was found in nonsynonymous substitutions in putatively targeted epitope regions (p-value <3 × 10−6), corresponding to 5.5 excess nonsynonymous substitutions.
source: We found a significant enrichment by a factor 1.9 in the putatively targeted region (p-value <3 × 10−6), corresponding to 5.5 excess nonsynonymous substitutions, whereby the total number of nonsynonymous substitutions per patient is on average 43 (median, quartiles 36–64).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of CTL epitope predictions and observed substitutions.

claim: The fraction of sites where the founder nucleotide is replaced by a mutant during the infection is about ten-fold higher if the founder nucleotide differs from the group M consensus than if it is identical to the group M consensus.
source: This fraction is about ten-fold higher if the founder nucleotide differs from the group M consensus than if it is identical to the group M consensus.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Reversion towards group M consensus occurs at a roughly constant rate throughout the observation time (5–8 years).
source: Reversion towards group M consensus occurs at a roughly constant rate throughout the observation time (5–8 years).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Of all changes accumulated by the viral populations, 30 ± 2.5% are reversions towards group M consensus.
source: Of all changes accumulated by the viral populations, 30 ± 2.5% are reversions towards group M consensus (mean and standard deviation of patient bootstraps after 4–7 years).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Reversions are between 4 and 5 times more frequent than expected in the absence of a reversion bias.
source: Reversions are between 4 and 5 times more frequent than expected in the absence of a reversion bias (7.8 and 4.5%, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with expected values.

claim: The rate of reversion is highest at the most conserved sites.
source: We find that the rate of reversion is highest at the most conserved sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Almost 50% of all non-consensus positions at highly conserved sites had reverted to consensus after about 5 years – an almost 1000-fold excess.
source: Almost 50% of all non-consensus positions at highly conserved sites had reverted to consensus after about 5 years – an almost 1000-fold excess.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Even at the least conserved sites, divergence towards group M consensus exceeded divergence away from group M consensus by a factor of 3.
source: Even at the least conserved sites, divergence towards group M consensus exceeded divergence away from group M consensus by a factor of 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: For most fragments, linkage disequilibrium shows a consistent decrease over the first 100–200 bps.
source: For most fragments, we observed a consistent decrease of LD over the first 100–200 bps, with fragment 5 being an exception with linkage of mutations at longer distances.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The linkage control (a 50/50 mix of two distinct virus isolates) shows no decay of LD with distance, suggesting negligible RT-PCR recombination.
source: Importantly, our linkage control (a 50/50 mix of two distinct virus isolates and a total of 1250 RNA molecules per PCR fragment) shows no decay of LD with distance, suggesting negligible RT-PCR recombination.
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The observed decay of LD in patient samples is consistent with a recombination rate of 10−5/bp/day.
source: The observed decay of LD in patient samples is consistent with a recombination rate of 10−5/bp/day as estimated in (Batorsky et al., 2011; Neher and Leitner, 2010).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data and comparison with published estimates.

claim: Intrapatient diversity recapitulates diversity seen across HIV-1 group M.
source: Our observation that intrapatient diversity recapitulates diversity seen across HIV-1 group M and the strong tendency to revert towards consensus suggest that, in chronic infection, selection determines diversity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and represents an inference from the results.

claim: Mutations further apart than 100 bp are effectively shuffled by recombination in most parts of genome.
source: We observe that mutations further apart than 100 bp are effectively shuffled by recombination in most parts of genome, consistent with previous estimates of the HIV-1 recombination rate (Batorsky et al., 2011; Neher and Leitner, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and citations to previous work.

claim: The bias towards reversion results in a two- to three-fold reduction of the long-term evolutionary rate of HIV.
source: The bias towards reversion results in a two- to three-fold reduction of the long-term evolutionary rate of HIV, a trend that is reinforced by selection during transmission (Carlson et al., 2014; Sagar et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the reversion data and is supported by citations.

claim: Inter-individual evolutionary rates of HIV-1 are two to six times lower than intra-individual rates.
source: Inter-individual evolutionary rates of HIV-1 are two to six times lower than intra-individual rates, and a number of possible mechanisms have been suggested to explain this discrepancy (Lythgoe and Fraser, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lythgoe and Fraser, 2012.

claim: Most of the mismatch between inter-individual and intra-individual evolutionary rates can be explained by steady reversion during infection.
source: Our results strongly indicate that most of this mismatch can be explained by steady reversion during infection; other factors such as retrieval of 'stored' latent variants or stage-specific selection might also contribute to the rate mismatch (Immonen and Leitner, 2014; Lythgoe and Fraser, 2012).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the reversion data presented in the study.

claim: The global HIV-1 group M consensus sequence represents an 'optimal' HIV-1 sequence, which acts as an attractor for the evolutionary dynamics within hosts.
source: These results suggest that the global HIV-1 group M consensus sequence represents an 'optimal' HIV-1 sequence, which acts as an attractor for the evolutionary dynamics within hosts.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the reversion data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The reproducible exploration of sequence space can coexist with frequent adaptation only in frequently recombining large populations.
source: The reproducible exploration of sequence space can coexist with frequent adaptation only in frequently recombining large populations (Neher et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Neher et al., 2013.

claim: Linkage and stochastic effects become stronger with increasing frequency of strength of selection, consistent with lower synonymous diversity and more LD in env.
source: Linkage and stochastic effects become stronger with increasing frequency of strength of selection, consistent with lower synonymous diversity and more LD in env.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Reversion is not limited to early infection but happens throughout chronic infection.
source: While reversion is particularly prevalent in acute infection (Li et al., 2007), we show that reversion is not limited to early infection but happens throughout chronic infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and a citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: Cross-sectional conservation has been used as a proxy for fitness costs in models of HIV-1 fitness landscapes.
source: Recently, cross-sectional conservation has been used as a proxy for fitness costs in models of HIV-1 fitness landscapes (Dahirel et al., 2011; Ferguson et al., 2013; Mann et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Reproducible intrapatient diversity likely reflects fitness costs of mutations in vivo, providing a direct justification for using cross-sectional conservation as a proxy for fitness costs.
source: Since reproducible intrapatient diversity likely reflects fitness costs of mutations in vivo, our results provide a direct justification for this approach.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data showing reproducible patterns of diversity.

claim: The majority of patients were MSM infected with subtype B virus.
source: The majority of patients were MSM infected with subtype B virus.
evidence: The claim describes the composition of the study cohort as shown in Table 1.

claim: The number of available template molecules was small in some samples.
source: While substitution and recombination errors of our optimized protocol for HIV-1 RNA extraction and an RT-PCR are low, the other main limitation was that the number of available template molecules was small in some samples (see also Iyer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the study and is supported by data in Figure 9.

claim: All read files have been uploaded to ENA with study accession number PRJEB9618.
source: All read files have been uploaded to ENA with study accession number PRJEB9618.
evidence: The claim provides information about data availability.

claim: Sequencing libraries were made starting from 0.1–1.5 ng of DNA with a stringent size selection for long inserts (>400 bp).
source: Sequencing libraries were made starting from 0.1–1.5 ng of DNA with a stringent size selection for long inserts (>400 bp).
evidence: The claim describes the library preparation methodology.

claim: The coverage varied considerably between samples and amplicons, but was mostly of the order of several thousands or more.
source: The coverage varied considerably between samples and amplicons, but was mostly of the order of several thousands or more, see Figure 1B.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Template availability, rather than coverage, determined the sequencing depth.
source: Hence template availability, rather than coverage, determined the sequencing depth, see Figure 1B.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of template numbers and coverage shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Frequency estimates were often reproducible to within a few percent.
source: Frequency estimates were often reproducible to within a few percent.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of SNP frequencies in overlapping fragments.

claim: Depending on the sample and fragment, SNP frequencies could be estimated down to 1% accuracy (corresponding to several hundred effective templates).
source: Taken together, our control experiments show that depending on the sample and fragment, we could estimate frequencies of SNPs down to 1% accuracy (corresponding to several hundred effective templates).
evidence: The claim summarizes the accuracy of the sequencing approach based on control experiments.

claim: SNPs remained linked through cDNA synthesis, PCR and sequencing.
source: Furthermore, SNPs remained linked through cDNA synthesis, PCR and sequencing.
evidence: The claim describes a property of the sequencing methodology that enables haplotype analysis.

claim: The application allows browsing the data either by patient or by genomic region and provides composite interactive plots to explore how the virus population has changed over time.
source: The application allows browsing the data either by patient or by genomic region and provides composite interactive plots to explore how the virus population has changed over time.
evidence: The claim describes features of the web application developed for the study.

claim: Some regions such as the variable loops in gp120 and nef evolve faster, while enzymes – protease (PR), reverse transcriptase (RT) – and the rev response element (RRE) evolve more slowly.
source: As expected, some regions such as the variable loops in gp120 and nef evolve faster, while enzymes – protease (PR), reverse transcriptase (RT) – and the rev response element (RRE) evolve more slowly.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Frequent recombination allows the viral population to evolve independently in different regions of the genome.
source: We further find frequent recombination, which allows the viral population to evolve independently in different regions of the genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Recombination is not frequent enough to decouple mutations closer than 100 base pairs.
source: Nevertheless, recombination is not frequent enough to decouple mutations closer than 100 base pairs and we observe signatures of hitch-hiking at short distances (Maynard Smith and Haigh, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and a citation.

claim: The first sample is estimated to be between 1 and 7 months into infection.
source: Our first sample is estimated to be between 1 and 7 months into infection and a few mutations (likely CTL escape mutations) had probably spread through the viral population by that time.
evidence: The claim is based on the estimated dates of infection and sampling times.

claim: The initial consensus sequence probably will differ slightly from the true founder virus.
source: Thus, the initial consensus sequence probably will differ slightly from the true founder virus.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the timing of the first sample.

claim: The number of differences between the initial consensus and the true founder will be small compared to the sequence divergence in the 5 or more years of follow-up.
source: The number of differences, however, will be small compared to the sequence divergence in the 5 or more years of follow-up such that this initial consensus sequence is a useful approximation of the founder virus(es).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the relative time scales of early evolution and the follow-up period.

claim: Variation is not limited by the mutational input, but HIV-1 populations accumulate diversity wherever mutations do not severely compromise virus replication.
source: Taken together, the observations in Figure 4 show that variation is not limited by the mutational input, but that HIV-1 populations accumulate diversity wherever mutations do not severely compromise virus replication.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the single nucleotide level, the spectrum of mutational possibilities is explored reproducibly and the level of within-host diversity is predicted by time since infection and cross-sectional diversity.
source: At the single nucleotide level, the spectrum of mutational possibilities is explored reproducibly and the level of within-host diversity is predicted by time since infection and cross-sectional diversity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Conserved positions are typically monomorphic even in deeply sequenced samples with high RNA template input.
source: Conserved positions are typically monomorphic even in deeply sequenced samples with high RNA template input.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Frequent nonsynonymous substitutions limit synonymous diversity because they drive linked synonymous mutations to fixation or to extinction.
source: This suggests that frequent non-synonymous substitutions limit synonymous diversity because they drive linked synonymous mutations to fixation or to extinction (Maynard Smith and Haigh, 1974).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the anti-correlation observed in Figure 5C and is supported by a citation.

claim: Due to substantial recombination, sweeping nonsynonymous mutations only occasionally 'drag' adjacent synonymous mutations to fixation.
source: This corroborates the interpretation that, due to substantial recombination, sweeping nonsynonymous mutations only occasionally 'drag' adjacent synonymous mutations to fixation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the site frequency spectrum data in Figure 5D.

claim: Synonymous mutations rarely rise in frequency because of their own effect on fitness, since they usually have small or deleterious phenotypic effects and do not contribute directly in immune evasion.
source: Synonymous mutations rarely rise in frequency because of their own effect on fitness, since they usually have small or deleterious phenotypic effects and do not contribute directly in immune evasion (Zanini and Neher, 2013).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: The total number of nonsynonymous substitutions per patient is on average 43 (median, quartiles 36–64).
source: We found a significant enrichment by a factor 1.9 in the putatively targeted region (p-value <3 × 10−6), corresponding to 5.5 excess nonsynonymous substitutions, whereby the total number of nonsynonymous substitutions per patient is on average 43 (median, quartiles 36–64).
evidence: The claim reports a measured value from the data analysis.

claim: The actual number of CTL driven substitutions could be higher than the 5.5 excess nonsynonymous substitutions found in predicted epitopes.
source: The set of predicted epitopes will contain false positives and lack true epitopes, hence the actual number of CTL driven substitutions could be higher as for example suggested by Allen et al. (2005) who report that roughly half of non-envelope mutations are associated with CTL responses.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on limitations of the epitope prediction method and is supported by a citation.

claim: The balance between escape and reversion results in association between specific escape mutations and the HLA types of the hosts.
source: The balance between escape and reversion results in association between specific escape mutations and the HLA types of the hosts (Kawashima et al., 2009; Palmer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In a diverse population of hosts, the most common state at a specific site is likely the preferred state, while rare alleles tend to be escape mutations that reduce viral replicative capacity.
source: In a diverse population of hosts, the most common state at a specific site is likely the preferred state, while rare alleles tend to be escape mutations that reduce viral replicative capacity (Carlson et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: These findings agree with results by Allen et al. (2005), who report that about 20% of amino acid substitutions are reversions.
source: These findings agree with results by Allen et al. (2005), who report that about 20% of amino acid substitutions are reversions.
evidence: The claim compares the study results with previous work.

claim: This attraction is strongest at conserved sites, but extends to the least conserved sites in the genome.
source: This attraction is strongest at conserved sites, but extends to the least conserved sites in the genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Given the five-fold excess of reverting minor variation, reversion would balance divergence once the typical distance from the consensus sequence equals 17%, corresponding to a nucleotide diversity of about 30%.
source: Given the five-fold excess of reverting minor variation, reversion would balance divergence once the typical distance from the consensus sequence equals 17%, corresponding to a nucleotide diversity of about 30%; this is remarkably close to the actual divergence between HIV-1 groups M, N and O (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a calculation based on the observed reversion rate and is supported by a citation.

claim: This apparent deceleration of evolution could explain the contradictory findings of attempts to date the age of HIV-1 and SIV.
source: This apparent deceleration of evolution could explain the contradictory findings of attempts to date the age of HIV-1 and SIV (Worobey et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is speculation supported by a citation.

claim: The strong and lasting preference for specific nucleotides needs to be accounted for in phylogenetic analysis.
source: The strong and lasting preference for specific nucleotides needs to be accounted for in phylogenetic analysis, as has recently been shown using experimentally determined fitness landscapes of influenza virus proteins (Bloom, 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: The observations are consistent with results by Ashenberg et al. (2013); Doud et al. (2015), who showed that amino acid preferences are mostly conserved between related influenza strains.
source: Our observations are consistent with results by Ashenberg et al. (2013); Doud et al. (2015), who showed that amino acid preferences are mostly conserved between related influenza strains.
evidence: The claim compares the study results with previous work on influenza.

claim: Divergence between HIV-1 subtypes is small enough that epistatic interactions have not yet changed the majority of the preferred states.
source: Similarly, divergence between HIV-1 subtypes is small enough that epistatic interactions have not yet changed the majority of the preferred states.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed conservation of preferences.

claim: With increasing evolutionary distance between strains, the molecular context and preferred amino acid at a particular position is more and more likely to differ.
source: With increasing evolutionary distance between strains, the molecular context and preferred amino acid at a particular position is more and more likely to differ (Pollock et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation.

claim: A subset of amino acids preferences are conserved almost universally and enable sequence based homology search.
source: Nevertheless, a subset of amino acids preferences are conserved almost universally (Risso et al., 2015) and enable sequence based homology search.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The concordance between intrahost variation and patterns of conservation across HIV-1 group M hints at universal fitness costs of mutations.
source: The concordance between intrahost variation and patterns of conservation across HIV-1 group M hints at universal fitness costs of mutations.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nine patients are insufficient to extend the analysis to fitness interactions between mutations.
source: However, nine patients are insufficient to extend this analysis to fitness interactions between mutations.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: The Primer ID method allows quantification of templates and almost complete elimination of experimental substitution and recombination errors.
source: In principle, the Primer ID method, which labels and resequences each individual template, allows quantification of templates and almost complete elimination of experimental substitution and recombination errors (Jabara et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Primer ID method.

claim: There is no standardized Primer ID protocol for genome-wide sequencing.
source: However, we are not aware of a Primer ID protocol for genome-wide sequencing, which was essential to our study.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of available methods.

claim: The limiting factor for adaptation is not generating the useful mutations, but combining multiple mutations necessary to survive and pruning deleterious mutations.
